claims.text: Machine-learning-optimized annealing schedules can control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Such control occurs by balancing competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors governing phase nucleation and growth.
The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy may be produced by conventional casting or powder processes.
The initial alloy contains a mixture of equilibrium and metastable phases.
A machine-learning-driven method can integrate experimental and computational datasets for HEA design or processing.
The integrated method can predict optimized annealing temperatures, hold times, and cooling rates.
Laboratory thermal processing permits precise control of temperature, dwell time, and cooling rate.
Thermal processing determines phase nucleation and growth kinetics, ordering, and precipitation behavior.
Historical experimental data and CALPHAD predictions can be processed to identify optimal thermal schedules.
Optimized thermal schedules modulate the balance between thermodynamic stability and kinetic accessibility.
Optimized schedules selectively enhance or suppress nucleation of desired equilibrium phases.
Optimized schedules minimize unwanted metastable-phase formation.
ML-optimized annealing produces a more uniform and targeted phase distribution than conventional thermal treatment.
ML-optimized annealing improves phase purity relative to conventional treatment.
ML-optimized annealing enhances mechanical properties relative to conventional treatment.
Standard heat treatments that do not account for coupled kinetic and thermodynamic parameters lead to unpredictable multiphase microstructures.
The effectiveness of the method is limited by the quality of available data.
The effectiveness of the method depends on the comprehensiveness of computational models and CALPHAD databases.
Variations in alloy composition or processing equipment may reduce reproducibility.
Predictive accuracy in new processing regimes and scalability across Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni compositional variants remain uncertain.
